newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Bolger needs foe's backing to avoid defeat.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Bolger needs foe's backing to avoid defeat.

text.p: New Zealand Prime Minister Jim Bolger's conservative National government is staring at defeat in a general election on Saturday after a huge lead in the polls has evaporated over the past three weeks.
Ironically, his fate hinges on whether one of his bitterest rivals decides to back him.
On current polling, the Maori leader of the nationalist New Zealand First Party, Winston Peters -- whom Bolger dumped from cabinet in 1991 -- will hold the balance of power.
An average of the latest three polls shows National with 32.3 percent, Labour with 26.5, Alliance with 14.2 and New Zealand First with 14.7.

Although National is still likely to be the biggest party, Labour-New Zealand First is seen as the likeliest coalition. But if Peters jumps the other way and joins a National-led coalition, he returns the government to power. Alliance has ruled itself out of a post-election coalition.
Bolger, a stolid 61-year-old farmer of Irish Catholic ancestry who left school at 15, has campaigned on the stability of his government against a divided opposition.

But business leaders have generally offered only lukewarm support, leaving Bolger looking alarmist and almost unpatriotic as he warns of "the crash of '97" and a "Sunday, bloody Sunday" on October 13 if the left wins power.
Bolger, a father of nine, has never been a populist leader since becoming prime minister in a landslide victory in 1990.

Yet he has shown he can hold his own on the world stage. He was outspoken in his condemnation of French nuclear tests in the South Pacific last year, when he led a chorus of opposition from regional leaders.

His firm stewardship helped to avert a crisis in the Commonwealth last November when Nigeria hanged nine human rights activists during a summit of the 52-nation group in Auckland. Members voted promptly to suspend the African state.
At home, Bolger has skilfully adjusted to a sea change in New Zealand politics with the switch from British-style first-past-the-post to a German-style proportional system.

Few expected him to see out his second three-year term after snatching a one-seat majority from the 1993 election. But Bolger survived, leading majority, minority and coalition governments by turn as some of his MPs defected to form new parties.
From a deep recession in the late 1980s and early 1990s, economic growth rebounded, unemployment fell to six percent, and a series of budget surpluses have allowed tax to be cut.
But there is a groundswell of opinion that 12 years of economic reforms have widened the gap between rich and poor.
The lack of a strong and reliable coalition partner has made Bolger's National Party look vulnerable, and he has been heavily criticised for running a negative campaign.

Bolger may need to swallow his pride and make overtures to New Zealand First's Peters when bargaining starts on forming a coalition. There will be no room for arrogance, a trait Bolger's minders have worried about in the past.

Yet he has also shown great flexibility by moving National from an opponent of New Zealand's anti-nuclear legislation to its greatest defender, and from a detractor of Nelson Mandela's African National Congress to a friend of the new South Africa.
He will need all that flexibility to survive if the polls are borne out.
